set.summary: After the attempted assassination of Ambassador Shlomo Argov in London by the Abu Nidal group, Israel invaded Lebanon on 6 June 1982. The cabinet had approved an operation to push the PLO about 40 km from the border; according to Schiff and Ya'ari, Defence Minister Sharon expanded it step by step, fighting Syrian forces and besieging West Beirut until PLO fighters were evacuated in August-September. Lebanese police figures reported in December 1982 counted 19,085 people killed and 30,302 wounded between 4 June and 31 August 1982, fighters included; in Beirut 84 percent of the 6,775 dead were civilians. Sharon disputed media casualty figures, speaking in late August of some 2,000 civilian casualties. On the Israeli side the army reported 269 soldiers killed in the first 20 days, Sharon gave 350 for the operation, the army counted 446 by 19 November 1982, and Israel Radio's count of Israelis killed in Lebanon reached 478 by May 1983.

affected_populations.note: Sharon (JTA, 30 Aug 1982): 350 killed and 2,000 wounded during the operation; Israeli army (CSM, 21 Dec 1982): 446 killed and 2,383 wounded by 19 Nov 1982; Israel Radio count (JTA, 2 May 1983): 478 killed and 2,614 wounded since June 1982. The army's figure for the first 20 days (to 26 June) was 269 killed (JTA, 30 June 1982).

Lebanese police count for 4 June-31 Aug 1982 as reported by the Christian Science Monitor (21 Dec 1982); includes Palestinian, Syrian and Lebanese fighters. In Beirut 6,775 died, 84 percent of them civilians; in southern Lebanon about 20 percent of the dead were civilians. Sharon (JTA, 30 Aug 1982) put civilian casualties at some 2,000.
No separate sourced figure; Syrian fighters are included in the Lebanese police count above.

set.summary: Between 16 and 18 September 1982 Lebanese Phalangist militiamen, admitted by the IDF into the Sabra neighbourhood and Shatila refugee camp in Israeli-controlled West Beirut, killed civilians, mainly Palestinians and Lebanese; Iranians, Syrians, Pakistanis and Algerians were also among the dead. Estimates of the toll range from roughly 300 to 3,000: the official Red Cross burial counted 328 bodies; Lebanon's prosecutor general reported 597 bodies found and 2,000 people missing; the IDF estimated 700-800 killed; other estimates put the dead at about 1,000; and one Israeli source put the number of civilians killed at 3,000. The killings caused a political crisis in Israel.

affected_populations.note: Range of estimates (Malone, Utah L. Rev. 1985): Red Cross burial count 328; IDF 700-800; about 1,000; one Israeli source 3,000. Lebanese prosecutor general (24 Sep 1982): 597 bodies found, 2,000 missing.

set.summary: On the night of 25 September 1982 a mass rally in Tel Aviv, organised by the Labor Alignment, the Shinui party and Peace Now, protested the Sabra and Shatila massacre and the government's refusal to set up a full independent inquiry; speakers called for the resignations of Prime Minister Begin and Defence Minister Sharon. Crowd figures were contested: the organisers gave the New York Times a figure of 350,000 and claimed to JTA 'over 400,000', while police declined to give an estimate but called it one of the largest rallies ever held. The government appointed the Kahan Commission days later.

add_cite.quote: Organizers of the rally said the crowd numbered 350,000; the country has a population of about four million.

add_cite.claim: speakers called for Begin's and Sharon's resignation and an independent judicial inquiry
add_cite.quote: Rallying in a plaza before City Hall here, the throng gave thunderous roars of applause and cheers to speakers who called on Mr. Begin and his Defense Minister, Ariel Sharon, to resign. Equally raucous eruptions greeted calls for the creation of an independent judicial inquiry commission to assess the Israeli role in the massacre

add_cite.quote: Last Saturday night’s rally here to protest the massacre of Palestinians in two refugee camps in west Beirut and the government’s refusal (at that point) to launch a full independent investigation of the carnage was the largest rally ever to have taken place in Israel, either in support of or in opposition to government policies.

Police declined to give on estimate of attendance, but said it was “one of the largest” rallies to have been held.

set.summary: Three days after the Coastal Road attack Israel invaded southern Lebanon against PLO bases and within days occupied the south up to the Litani River, except Tyre and its surroundings. On 15 March Lebanon protested to the Security Council that it had no connection with the commando raid, reporting that an undetermined number of Lebanese citizens had been killed, notably in Tyre, and that large numbers of people were fleeing the south. On 19 March the Security Council (resolution 425) called on Israel to withdraw and created UNIFIL.

set.summary: Eight Israeli F-16s escorted by F-15s destroyed the Osirak (Tammuz) research reactor, under construction by French technicians near Baghdad, on 7 June 1981. Israel said the reactor would have become operational within months and could produce nuclear weapons; Labor's Mordechai Gur argued it was not as close to completion as Prime Minister Begin had suggested. French sources said one French technician was killed, while Israel's communique said no technicians were on the site. The Security Council unanimously condemned the attack in resolution 487 and the United States briefly suspended F-16 deliveries.

affected_populations.note: No Iraqi casualty figure found in an opened source.
French sources (JTA, June 1981): one French technician killed; Israel's communique said no technicians were on site and none were hurt.

remove_claims: ten Iraqi soldiers and a French technician were killed

The communique said the attack was based on positive knowledge from unimpeachable sources that the Iraqi reactor would be operational between early July and early September and could produce nuclear weapons intended for use against Israel.

set.summary: The state commission of inquiry headed by Supreme Court President Yitzhak Kahan made its report public on 8-9 February 1983. It found Israel indirectly responsible for the Sabra and Shatila killings and Defence Minister Ariel Sharon personally responsible for disregarding the danger of bloodshed, and recommended that he resign or be dismissed. The cabinet voted 16-1 to accept the recommendations, Sharon casting the only vote against; he left the defence ministry but remained in the cabinet as minister without portfolio.

add_cite.quote: The commission, in its report and recommendations published here this morning, accepted Begin’s testimony that he knew nothing of the massacres until he heard of them from a foreign radio broadcast after the fact.

add_cite.claim: date: Malone dates the commission's conclusions 9 February 1983
add_cite.quote: On February 9, 1983, an Israeli commission of inquiry into the massacres concluded that the State of Israel and several individual Israelis, including Ariel Sharon, were "indirectly" responsible for the massacres.

add_cite.claim: recommended that Sharon resign or be dismissed
add_cite.quote: The commission recommended that if Sharon does not resign, Premier Menachem Begin should exercise his statutory authority and dismiss him.

add_cite.claim: the cabinet voted 16-1 to accept the recommendations, Sharon casting the only vote against
add_cite.quote: The Cabinet voted 16-1 tonight to accept in full the report and recommendations of the commission of inquiry into the Beirut refugee camps massacre. Defense Minister Ariel Sharon, whose resignation was called for by the commission, cast the lone dissenting vote.

set.summary: Eleven Fatah gunmen who landed by boat hijacked a bus on the coastal highway on 11 March 1978. Prime Minister Begin said 37 Israeli civilians were killed and 76 wounded; a later report put the wounded at 82. Two of the attackers were captured and later tried; the other nine were killed.

set.summary: After 13 days of talks hosted by US President Carter, Begin and Sadat signed two frameworks on 17 September 1978: one for an Egypt-Israel peace treaty based on full Israeli withdrawal from Sinai, and one for Palestinian autonomy in the West Bank and Gaza; the autonomy negotiations were still deadlocked in 1982. Begin agreed to let the Knesset decide on evacuating the Sinai settlements.

add_cite.quote: One of the major elements of the accords was a framework for autonomy for the Palestinians on the West Bank and Gaza. By year’s end, however, the negotiations had not moved beyond the point where they were deadlocked three years ago, and Egypt, under President Hosni Mubarak, was balking at resuming the autonomy talks.

patches.why: #242 drop: 'never implemented' replaced by sourced 'autonomy negotiations still deadlocked in 1982' (JTA highlights 5742). #244 concerns a choice note - choices untouched.

set.summary: On 2 June 1980, a month after six yeshiva students were killed in an ambush in Hebron, car bombs planted by members of a Jewish settler underground maimed the mayors of Nablus, Bassam Shakaa, who lost both legs, and Ramallah, Karim Khalaf; a police sapper was injured dismantling a bomb intended for a third mayor. The attack was believed to be a reprisal for the Hebron killings. The perpetrators were identified only in 1984.

set.summary: Bashir Gemayel, the Phalange leader elected president of Lebanon on 23 August 1982 with Israeli backing, was killed on 14 September 1982 when a bomb destroyed the Phalangist party headquarters in east Beirut; first reports put eight others dead and at least 50 injured. A later JTA account attributed the killing, 'presumably', to the Syrians. The IDF entered West Beirut the next day.

set.summary: An explosion destroyed the Israeli military headquarters in Tyre on 11 November 1982, killing 76 Israeli soldiers, Shin Bet agents and Border Police and 15 Lebanese detainees (2024 figures; earlier counts of detainees varied). Israel long attributed the blast to gas cylinders; a 2024 IDF inquiry found a car bomb 'highly probable'. A truck bomb at the Israeli headquarters in Tyre on 4 November 1983 killed 29 Israeli service personnel and 31 Lebanese, according to JTA.

set.summary: Israel's major banks had for years propped up their own share prices. When the shares began to collapse, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange closed from 6 October 1983 for about two weeks, and the government undertook to buy bank shares from the public, effectively nationalising the main banks. The Bejski Commission reported on the affair in April 1986.

set.summary: Four Palestinians from the Gaza Strip hijacked an Egged bus on 12 April 1984. In the rescue the next morning an Israeli soldier, Irit Portuguez, was killed and seven passengers were wounded; two hijackers were killed and two captured alive, who were then killed on the orders of Shin Bet chief Avraham Shalom. A press photograph exposed the cover-up; Shalom and other officers received presidential pardons in 1986.

set.summary: The Shin Bet arrested members of a settler underground in late April 1984 after they planted bombs on Arab buses in East Jerusalem. The group was responsible for the 1980 car bombings of West Bank mayors and the July 1983 attack on the Islamic College in Hebron that killed three students and wounded about 30-33, and had planned to blow up the Dome of the Rock.

set.summary: Between 21 November 1984 and 5 January 1985 some 7,600 Ethiopian Jews who had trekked to refugee camps in Sudan were airlifted to Israel on dozens of night flights over 45 days. Reports in January 1985, quoting Sudanese officials and relief workers, said at least 2,000 Ethiopian Jews had died in the Sudanese camps, including nearly 1,800 of 7,000 at the Umm Rekuba camp. The airlift stopped after it became public; according to President Weizman, the United States also brought about 600 Jews out of the Sudanese camps in cargo planes.

set.summary: On 14 January 1985 the cabinet voted 16-6 for a three-stage withdrawal from south Lebanon. The IDF pulled back in stages, and by the third anniversary of the invasion in June 1985 the war ended without any announcement, leaving a 'security belt' along the border held by the South Lebanon Army with IDF liaison officers. The war had cost 654 Israeli soldiers and other security personnel dead and nearly 6,000 wounded. The zone's Lebanese residents lived under the control of the SLA and the IDF, and human-rights groups documented shelling of villages around it.

set.summary: Israel and the United States signed the first US free-trade agreement in April 1985 (Industry Minister Ariel Sharon and US Trade Representative William Brock); it took effect on 1 September 1985. Duties were phased down over a decade, with the stated goal that all trade between the two countries would be duty-free by 1995.

set.summary: With inflation running at several hundred percent a year (380.75% in the twelve months to June 1985), the unity government adopted an emergency stabilisation plan on 1 July 1985: an 18.8 percent devaluation that set the shekel at 1,500 to the dollar, deep subsidy and budget cuts, a three-month freeze on prices, wages and salaries, and a wage agreement with the Histadrut; in July the government printed no new money. Inflation plunged from 285% in 1985 to 18% in 1986.

add_cite.claim: inflation of 380.75% in the twelve months to June 1985
add_cite.quote: The figures, made public here, are for the period June 30, 1985-June 30, 1986. The rate for the previous 12-month period was 380.75 percent.

add_cite.claim: in July 1985 the government printed no new money
add_cite.quote: During July, too, for the first time, this year, not only did the government not print any new money, but in fact absorbed from the public some $170 million, he reported.

patches.why: #303 drop: 'fixed exchange rate' replaced by the sourced rate-setting devaluation (1,500 to $1, S1403); 'limits on central-bank financing' replaced by JTA's 'printed no new money' in July 1985. #304 fix: 445% -> 380.75% for the year to June 1985 (JTA).

set.summary: In late August 1985 the cabinet approved removing the last three zeros from the shekel: new shekel notes and coins, each new shekel worth 1,000 old ones, went into circulation within days, and old and new shekels were both valid until 1 January 1986. Finance Minister Yitzhak Modai called the change purely technical, made necessary by inflation.

add_cite.claim: date August 1985: cabinet approved removing three zeros; new notes and coins into circulation that week; both valid until 1 January
add_cite.quote: The Cabinet accepted a proposal today to introduce a technical change in the value of the Shekel, by removing the last three zeros from the face value of the currency. The exchange rate this weekend was 1,480 Shekels to the U.S. dollar. New notes and coins will go into circulation this Wednesday. In an interim period until January I, both the old and new Shekels will be valid in the market.

add_cite.claim: Modai called the change purely technical
add_cite.quote: Finance Minister Yitzhak Modai said at a press conference today that the purpose of the change was purely technical.

patches.why: #309 drop: the 4 September 1985 date replaced by JTA's late-August cabinet decision with circulation 'this Wednesday' (date 1985-08-01, month precision, same turn).

set.summary: Days after three Israelis were killed on a yacht in Larnaca, Cyprus, Israeli aircraft bombed the PLO headquarters at Hammam Chott near Tunis on 1 October 1985. First reports from Tunis spoke of at least 15 dead and Israel's chief of staff Moshe Levy of 30-50; Tunisia told the Security Council that initial estimates were more than 60 dead and more than 100 injured, and that the area was residential, home to Tunisian families and Palestinian civilians. The Security Council condemned the raid in resolution 573, with the United States abstaining.

affected_populations.note: IDF chief of staff Levy: 30-50 killed (JTA, 2 Oct 1985); Tunisia: more than 50 dead and nearly 100 wounded (S/17509, 1 Oct), more than 60 dead and more than 100 injured (FM Caid Essebsi, S/PV.2610, 2 Oct). First reports from Tunis: at least 15.
Three Israelis killed in Larnaca before the raid.

remove_claims: reported deaths range from 47 to about 71, including PLO members and Tunisian civilians

add_cite.claim: first reports: at least 15 (Tunis) and 30-50 (IDF chief of staff Levy)
add_cite.quote: Reports from Tunis this morning said at least 15 persons were killed, presumably PLO terrorists. Reports from Tel Aviv quoted Israel's Chief of Staff Gen. Moshe Levy as saying 30-50 were killed and many more wounded.

add_cite.claim: Tunisia (1 Oct): more than 50 dead and nearly 100 wounded
add_cite.quote: 50 dead and nearly 100 wounded

add_cite.claim: Tunisian FM at the Security Council: more than 60 dead and more than 100 injured
add_cite.quote: That act of aggression resulted in the loss of many human lives, which initial estimates put at more than 60 dead and more than 100 injured.

add_cite.claim: Tunisia: the area was residential, home to Tunisian families and Palestinian civilians
add_cite.quote: the place chosen for this cowardly attack is situated in an exclusively residential urban area which has traditionally been the home of Tunisian families and a small number of Palestinian civilians

patches.why: #393 fix: 47-71 range replaced by attributed contemporary figures (Tunis 15+, Levy 30-50, Tunisia 50+/60+ via UN S/17509 and S/PV.2610); AP/effects [30,60].

set.summary: Following the interim withdrawal in Sinai, Israel and Egypt established full diplomatic relations and exchanged ambassadors in February 1980; an air-transport agreement between the two countries took effect the next month.

add_cite.claim: an air-transport agreement took effect in March 1980
add_cite.quote: The pact; signed on the eve of Passover, is in addition to the air-transportation agreement which went into effect last month, and is seen here as one more advance in the process of normalization.

patches.why: #292 drop: 'regular flights began the next month' replaced by the sourced air-transport agreement taking effect in March 1980 (JTA 3 Apr 1980).

set.summary: Katzrin was established on the Golan Heights in 1977. It grew into the main Israeli town there, described by JTA in the 1990s as 'the so-called capital of the Golan Heights'.

add_cite.claim: Katzrin became the so-called capital of the Golan Heights
add_cite.quote: On Saturday night, thousands of Golan settlers and their supporters rallied in the township of Katzrin, the so-called capital of the Golan Heights.

patches.why: #230 drop: 'planned urban centre ... following a government decision of November 1973' removed; replaced by JTA's description of Katzrin as the Golan's so-called capital.

set.summary: On the night of Thursday 7 April 1977 Maccabi Tel Aviv beat Varese of Italy 78-77 in Belgrade to win the European Cup championship game. Thousands of Israelis poured into the streets to celebrate, and Prime Minister Rabin delayed announcing his withdrawal from the election race by several hours because the country was watching the game.

add_cite.claim: date 1977-04-07 (Thursday night): Maccabi beat Varese 78-77 in the European Cup championship game in Belgrade
add_cite.quote: Premier Yitzhak Rabin’s announcement of his withdrawal as candidate for the May 17 elections was postponed for several hours Thursday night because Israelis were glued to their television sets watching a far more, for them, dramatic and important event: the victory of the Tel Aviv Maccabi basketball team over the Varese team of Italy in the European Cup championship game in Belgrade, Yugoslavia. When the 78-77 win for Israel was announced, thousands of joyous Israelis poured out of their homes onto the streets for a massive festival which continued until the early hours Friday.

patches.why: #287 drop rescued: score 78-77, opponent Varese, Belgrade, Thursday 7 April 1977 sourced to JTA 11 Apr 1977; 'first' title and sponsor name 'Mobilgirgi' removed (not in source).

set.summary: 'A-Ba-Ni-Bi' by Izhar Cohen and the Alphabeta won the Eurovision Song Contest in Paris on 22 April 1978 with 157 points, Israel's first win. When it was clear Israel would win, Jordan's broadcaster stopped its live transmission, citing technical difficulties.

remove_claims: place tel_aviv (event placed in Tel Aviv although the contest was in Paris)

add_cite.claim: contest held in Paris (place: abroad)
add_cite.quote: Venue & Location Palais des Congrès, Paris, France

add_cite.claim: Jordan's broadcaster stopped the live broadcast
add_cite.quote: When it was obvious that Israel would win, the broadcasting company of Jordan stopped the live broadcast claiming they had technical difficulties.

patches.why: #272 fix: place set to 'abroad' (contest in Paris, tel_aviv was only a map anchor); EBU's note on Jordan's broadcast added.

add_cite.claim: Milk and Honey with Gali Atari
add_cite.quote: The winning song was “Hollelujah,” sung by 26-year-old Gali Atari, who was accompanied by the Milk and Honey group.

set.summary: Hosting the contest in Jerusalem on 31 March 1979, Israel won again with 'Hallelujah' by Milk and Honey with Gali Atari, scoring 125 points.

patches.why: #275 drop rescued: Gali Atari sourced to JTA 2 Apr 1979; summary unchanged.

set.summary: Former Dimona technician Mordechai Vanunu gave The Sunday Times of London information and photographs of the Dimona nuclear facility, telling British newspapers in 1986 that Israel had a substantial arsenal of nuclear weapons. He was reported missing from London on 30 September 1986; he said he was lured to Rome, drugged and kidnapped by Israeli agents who brought him to Israel. He was convicted of treason and espionage in a trial closed to press and public in 1988 and sentenced to 18 years.

remove_claims: he had been lured to Rome and abducted by Mossad on 30 September

add_cite.claim: date 1986-09-30: reported missing from London; he said he was lured to Rome and kidnapped by Israeli agents
add_cite.quote: He was reported missing from London on Sept. 30, 1986. He claims he was lured to Rome, then drugged and kidnapped by Israeli agents who brought him to Israel against his will.

add_cite.claim: he told British newspapers Israel had a substantial nuclear arsenal
add_cite.quote: the fact that he told British newspapers earlier this year that Israel has a substantial arsenal of nuclear weapons.

patches.why: #399 drop: 5 October publication date removed (date set to his disappearance, 30 Sep 1986, turn 154); #400 fix: abduction presented as Vanunu's account, disappearance from London on 30 Sep.
